title: Maple and the Wobbly Bridge
markdown:
The moon was a sliver, a shy smile in the ink-blue sky, but the afternoon before it had been all sun. The old oak kept both their homes under its kindly branches. Maple was a bear of cinnamon fur and button eyes, the sort of friend who liked quiet afternoons by his burrow, the comforting scent of honey-milk, and the rustle of a favourite rhyme book. Gorse the goat kid lived next door, two smooth stones in one riverbed. Gorse was a whirlwind: fuzzy, bright, a spirit as bouncy as a dandelion seed, a white tail like a happy mark. He leaped. He bounded. Maple turned pages. They fitted anyway.

One sun-kissed afternoon they tumbled in a game of chase near the whispering woods, round the oak, through the clover-scented grass, Maple puffing and Gorse bleating with delight. Gorse’s bright eyes stopped first. “Look. Across the meadow. Lucky clover.”

A cluster sat in the emerald grass. Among it, Gorse’s sharp eyes found a perfect four-leaf. A tiny green star that had forgotten to stay in the sky.

Gorse’s hooves tap-tap-tapped. “I’d love one. Extra-sunny days. The sweetest berries.”

Maple smiled. Then he looked. Between them and the clover a brook chuckled over smooth stones. Across it, like a sleepy smile, lay a bridge of old weathered boards. A wobbly bridge. Maple’s whiskers trembled. His paws went damp as moss after rain. He pictured the boards dipping and swaying. His tummy did a somersault, a startled fish.

Gorse nudged him with a fuzzy head. “Come on. Just across. Think of the luck. It’ll be fun.” His eagerness was a little sunbeam. If they waited, the moon would peek and sleepy field mice would tuck the clover away. This was their chance.

Maple puffed his fluffy chest. “All right. Together.” Quiet, but his button eyes stayed steady.

They left the playing field where every blade felt like an old friend. The air hummed with water and tall grasses that tickled their noses. Wild flowers smelled sweet. A dragonfly stitched the air above the brook. The path still led to the crossing. Maple walked a little slower than Gorse, as if the meadow itself might change its mind and let them stay.

The boards, grey with age, some a bit loose, tilted and swayed and creaked. Gorse trotted to the edge with a confident hop. “See. Not so bad.”

Maple’s paw touched the first board. It dipped with a soft groan. Then it swayed. His heart flipped. His legs felt like jelly. He wanted his burrow and his blankets and no clover at all. He almost said he could not. He stood frozen, fur prickling.

Gorse looked back. “One step at a time. I’ll go first. You watch.” He trotted a little way on. The bridge wobbled. He did not fall. “The boards are strong enough. They just like to dance a bit.”

Maple watched. Really watched. Gorse was doing it. Maple thought of the green perfect clover, and of Gorse wanting it, and of Gorse being a little explorer. He put his paw on the next board. It wobbled. A tiny squeak escaped him. He did not stop. Another step. Another. Water chuckled under the gaps. A loose nail winked. He kept Gorse in his eyes, and the bright grass on the far side, and the solid path home in his mind. Mid-bridge he paused, just once, and Gorse waited without hurrying him. Then Maple went on.

The rough splintery wood dug into his paw. A low creak rose from the planks. Damp earthy brook-smell tickled his nose. He pushed down the flutter. This was the price: the wobbly path for the wish. One last slightly shaky step, and Maple was across. Firm ground. Relief, and a warm pride that was new. Gorse leaped, hooves clicking. “You did it. You were so brave.”

There, as Gorse had said, was the patch — greener than the rest of the meadow, cool under their feet. Gorse nosed among the three-leafs until he found the most perfect four-leaf, leaves delicate and smooth, and picked it carefully with his mouth so as not to bruise it. “For luck.” He held it so Maple could see the four little fans. Maple’s button eyes shone. The brook still chuckled behind them, but the clover was real, and so was the crossing.

Now home. The bridge still wobbled. Maple felt a flutter, but a smaller one — a reminder, not a wave. Gorse, clover held gentle, looked at him. “Ready?”

Maple looked at the friend who had believed when he had not. A loose board would creak. He could feel the sway just by looking. He would not be alone. “Yes. Let’s go home.”

He stepped on again, Gorse close, fuzzy side brushing cinnamon fur. A board dipped. Maple held his breath and did not freeze. He thought of dancing boards and put one paw carefully in front of the other. Halfway, the same loose board groaned as it had on the way out. Maple named it in his head — the dancer — and stepped as Gorse had shown him, steady, not a rush. They moved slowly. The creaks seemed less like warnings now. On the home bank Maple stood a moment longer than he needed, feeling the firm earth, then followed Gorse toward the oak.

They walked from the brook toward their homes, past the wild flowers and the dragonfly’s stitch, back to grass that felt like old friends. The sun dipped, orange and pink like warm brushstrokes. Maple felt a warmth better than honey-milk. When a gust made the old oak sway, he watched the branches dance and gave a quiet nod. Swaying things could be beautiful. Safe, even. Gorse laid the four-leaf on Maple’s rhyme book for a moment, then tucked it in a cup of water by the burrow door. The brook would keep chuckling, and the bridge would keep its little dance for the next time they needed luck.
characters: Maple (a teddy bear), Gorse (a goat kid)
